docs.title: LunCoSim Documentation
docs.text:
Open-source space mission workbench

First Drive in the View perspective. The tutorial card appears when a lesson starts.

This site is the user guide. It covers installation, the first lessons, and the concepts behind a LunCoSim project.

docs.title: Build a space mission.See how it behaves.
docs.text:
LunCoSim connects a USD scene, Modelica equations, and Rhai mission logic into one running system. Assemble a vehicle and its environment, then watch the mission behave.

Install LunCoSim Run your first lesson

docs.text:

    Download the desktop package for Windows, macOS, or Linux, then launch it.

    Install LunCoSim

  • Run your first lesson

    Open the Tutorials menu, take control of a rover, and complete a short guided exercise.

    First lesson

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Build and drive a rover. Assemble a vehicle, explore wheel and suspension behavior, and observe its interaction with terrain.
  • Connect equations to motion. Wire a Modelica controller to a rigid body and inspect the feedback loop while it runs.
  • Explore subsystem behavior. Edit electrical, thermal, and mechanical models in the embedded Modelica workbench and compare plots.
  • Script an operation. Define mission phases, waypoints, and responses to events, then inspect the resulting state in the UI or over the API.
  • Share a project. A Twin is an ordinary folder of USD, Modelica, Rhai, and configuration files that you can version and hand to a colleague.

docs.title: The four formats
docs.text:
Format Owns Typical files USD Scene structure, geometry, materials, physics schemas, typed ports and connections .usda, .usdc Modelica Continuous equations, state, and physical behavior .mo Rhai Events, commands, mission policy, and test verdicts .rhai TOML The Twin manifest and external asset declarations twin.toml, Assets.toml

The runtime projects those authored documents into a live world. Rust and Avian provide the generic engine mechanics; they are not where you author a particular rover, mission, or lesson.

docs.title: Assets.toml
docs.text:
Assets.toml declares external bytes that a Twin or the engine needs but does not store in the project: source libraries, terrain rasters, textures, fonts, and downloadable models.

It is a manifest, not a scene file and not a cache. The actual files are downloaded to a local cache and addressed from USD or Modelica through logical asset URIs.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• A Twin can have an Assets.toml at its root. Destinations resolve against the Twin.
  • The engine ships manifests under assets/manifests/*.toml using the same entry format. Each file is a group such as modelica, fonts, terrain, or celestial.

docs.title: A basic entry
docs.text:
[modelica_standard_library]
name = "Modelica Standard Library"
version = "4.1.0"
url = "https://github.com/modelica/ModelicaStandardLibrary/archive/refs/tags/v4.1.0.tar.gz"
dest = "library"
sha256 = "<sha256 of the archive>"

A single-file dataset uses the same shape:

[site_dem]
name = "Site terrain DEM"
url = "https://example.org/site-dem.tif"
dest = "assets/terrain/site-dem.tif"
sha256 = "<sha256 of the file>"

The table key is the asset key. It is what --asset / -a uses on the assets manager CLI.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning name Human-readable name used in progress and diagnostics url Download source dest Destination relative to the Twin root or engine cache version Version marker checked when validating an installed archive sha256 Expected content hash; the download is rejected on mismatch extract Archive-internal path to extract into dest shared Put the download in the shared global cache instead of the Twin-local cache recommended Offer the dataset during onboarding when it is missing process Optional processing recipe for a downloaded source bundle Binary names whose package should contain this artifact package_only Build-time package input, excluded from the runtime download catalog

dest is a portable relative path. Absolute paths, parent traversal, and platform-specific path syntax are rejected.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text:
A download can be followed by a processing step. A compound recipe uses kind = "pipeline" and must declare both the final artifacts and the ordered steps that produce them:

[site_dem.process]
kind = "pipeline"
output_root = "cache"
output = "terrain/site"
center_lat = -85.0
center_lon = 30.0
window_m = 1024.0
target_resolution = [257, 257]
frame = "MOON_ME"

[site_dem.process.pipeline]
artifacts = [
  { from = "height",
    source = "materials/textures/heightmap.tif",
    path = "materials/textures/heightmap.tif",
    kind = "dem",
    dimensions = [257, 257] },
]

[[site_dem.process.pipeline.steps]]
id = "height"
input = "source"
kind = "dem"
output = "height"

The artifacts table is the final consumer contract; a planner cannot replace it. A step input names source, another declared input, or an earlier step. Scratch outputs must be distinct and may not overlap.

Processing is optional. If the downloaded bytes are already the artifact you need, omit process.

docs.title: Runtime behavior
docs.text:
LunCoSim does not download in the background on launch. A missing declared dataset is shown to the user, and the download starts only after an explicit request. The same declarations are visible in Settings → Data & libraries and in the Twin's assets view.

The shared cache is:

Platform Default cache Linux ~/.cache/lunco/ macOS ~/Library/Caches/lunco/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\lunco\

Set LUNCOSIM_CACHE to override the cache root. Twin-scoped declarations write beside the Twin by default unless the entry is marked shared = true.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The assets manager in the source checkout can inspect and fetch a Twin's manifest:

cargo run -p lunco-assets -- list -t path/to/twin
cargo run -p lunco-assets -- download -t path/to/twin
cargo run -p lunco-assets -- process -t path/to/twin

Use -a <key> to target one entry, --force to replace an installed artifact, and --quality coarse|good to choose a faster or full processing bake.

docs.title: Addressing the result
docs.text:
Authored files never address the physical cache path. Use:

  • lunco://... for the installed engine asset library
  • twin://... for a file inside the open Twin

The asset registry resolves the logical URI to the installed bytes. A USD layer that hardcodes ~/.cache/lunco/... is not portable and does not use this contract.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text: LunCoSim separates what the system is from how it behaves and what the operation does. Each layer has a standard format and a clear owner.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
Layer Owns Does not own twin.toml Project identity, entry scene, search roots, settings Physical equations USD Parts, transforms, variants, materials, physics schemas, typed ports, connections Modelica state integration Modelica Continuous equations, energy/state balance, solved outputs Scene traversal or mission sequencing Rhai Events, commands, sequencing, authored test verdicts Continuous dynamics Assets.toml Declarations for external bytes: libraries, rasters, models, fonts Scene structure or runtime state Rust / Avian Generic projection, physics, scheduling, and engine mechanics A particular rover, mission, or lesson

The important rule is one fact, one owner. A wheel's position belongs in USD. A motor's torque curve belongs in Modelica. A waypoint mission belongs in Rhai. A downloaded terrain DEM belongs in Assets.toml and the asset cache.

docs.title: Runtime flow
docs.text:
1. The Twin opens. twin.toml selects the default USD scene and the Modelica and SysML source roots.
  2. USD composition resolves sublayers, references, payloads, and variants into one composed stage.
  3. The runtime projects the composed stage into the live entity world: scene hierarchy, transforms, physics bodies, colliders, lights, cameras, and program attachments.
  4. Modelica participants are admitted. The fixed master clock advances them; outputs cross SimConnections at declared communication points.
  5. Physics applies forces and integrates the rigid bodies. Rhai scenarios receive events and issue typed commands through the same command/query API as the UI and HTTP API.
  6. The UI renders the current state. The UI does not mutate domain state directly; it sends commands to the owning layer.

A composed USD stage by itself is inert. It does not launch Modelica, run Rhai, apply physics, or render. The runtime is what projects the authored documents into a live world.

docs.title: A rover, layer by layer
docs.text:
Question File What it contains Where is the chassis, where are the wheels, how do they attach? USD Xform hierarchy, references, UsdPhysics bodies and joints What is the controller law? Modelica .mo equations for drive, steering, motor, or thermal behavior What should the mission do? Rhai on_start, task, on_event, waypoints, commands, verdicts Where does the terrain DEM come from? Assets.toml URL, dest, optional sha256 and processing recipe Which scene opens? twin.toml [usd] default_scene

A complete drive loop can look like this:

USD                  Modelica                 Physics
wheels + joints  →   drive law + motor   →   forces + motion
      ↑                                           │
      └──────────── typed USD connections ─────────┘
                           │
                        Rhai policy
                 mission events and commands

docs.title: What stays out of each layer
docs.text:
• Do not put mission decisions or timers in Modelica.
  • Do not integrate physics or reimplement a controller in Rhai.
  • Do not encode equations in USD attributes.
  • Do not add a Rust special case for a specific rover, lesson, or asset.
  • Do not hand-edit generated or cached assets; author the source and let the owning pipeline produce the result.

Read the format pages next:

  • Twin — the project folder
  • twin.toml — the manifest
  • USD — the scene and topology
  • Modelica — continuous behavior
  • Rhai — scenario policy
  • Assets.toml — external assets

docs.title: Modelica
docs.text: Modelica is LunCoSim's language for continuous behavior: motion, power, thermal flow, fluid systems, and control laws. A .mo file contains equations, not a sequence of commands. The solver advances the equations over time.

docs.title: What Modelica owns
docs.text:
• Differential and algebraic equations
  • Continuous state and parameters
  • Acausal connections between physical ports
  • Inputs and outputs exchanged with physics or other domains
  • Solver-facing behavior at declared communication points

Modelica does not own scene traversal, mission sequencing, or user input. Those belong in USD and Rhai.

docs.title: A small model
docs.text:
within MyRover;

model Drive
  input Real throttle;
  output Real speed;
  parameter Real timeConstant = 1.0;

initial equation
  speed = 0.0;

equation
  der(speed) = (max(-1.0, min(1.0, throttle)) - speed) / timeConstant;
end Drive;

The pieces:

Keyword Meaning within MyRover; The package namespace for this class model Drive A reusable model class input Real throttle A value supplied by the surrounding system output Real speed A value exposed to the surrounding system parameter Real timeConstant A tunable value that is constant during a run initial equation The initial condition equation The continuous relationship der(speed) The time derivative of speed

This model turns a throttle command into a first-order speed response. It does not find prims, read the scene, or decide when a mission is complete.

docs.title: Attaching a model to USD
docs.text:
A Modelica class becomes a simulation participant when a USD prim carries LunCoProgramAPI and names the source:

def Scope "Controller" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
) {
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover/models/Drive.mo@
    uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true
}

Use @twin://...@ for a model inside the open Twin. Use @lunco://models/...@ for a model shipped in the installed asset library.

docs.title: How cosimulation works
docs.text:
When a Modelica model drives a physical body, LunCoSim runs the two sides together:

  1. The fixed master clock reaches a communication point.
  2. Model outputs are sampled.
  3. The values cross the authored USD connections as SimConnections.
  4. Physics applies the resulting forces or reads the new state.
  5. The new state becomes the next input sample.

Outputs are held between communication points. A script does not step this loop; the wiring and the runtime do. This is why a component must declare its outputs:<name> ports in USD before another component can consume them.

The rule of thumb:

  • Modelica owns the condition. A model computes low_fuel = 1 when its state crosses a threshold.
  • USD owns the wire. A LunCoEvent prim connects that output to a named event.
  • Rhai owns the response. A scenario listens for lander_low_fuel and displays a warning.

docs.title: The Lunica workbench
docs.text:
Open the Lunica perspective to work on Modelica directly. It provides the model browser, diagram view, equation view, parameter editing, compilation, run controls, plots, and experiments. See Perspectives for the layout and workflow.

Use it to:

  • inspect a model before attaching it to a scene
  • change parameters and compare runs
  • run a model in real time or as a fast batch
  • plot and compare experiment results

The simulator embeds the same workbench, so you do not need a separate application to edit a model used by a Twin.

docs.title: Practical rules
docs.text:
• Put equations and state in Modelica.
  • Put discrete decisions, mission phases, and event responses in Rhai.
  • Declare every value another component consumes as a USD outputs: property.
  • Keep parameters in the model or the manifest, not in a hidden script.
  • Recompile after changing a model; a stale artifact is not a valid run.

docs.title: Rhai
docs.text:
Rhai is LunCoSim's scripting language for scenario policy. A scenario is a persistent program attached to an entity. It observes the simulation, reacts to events, and issues typed commands. It does not integrate physics or replace a Modelica model.

Rhai is small, sandboxed, and implemented in Rust. The same scripts run on desktop and in the browser build.

docs.title: What Rhai owns
docs.text:
• Mission phases and objectives
  • Waypoint selection and sequencing
  • Reactions to events
  • User-facing hints, notifications, and tutorial flow
  • Authored test assertions and verdicts
  • Policy decisions that should be editable without rebuilding Rust

docs.title: What Rhai does not own
docs.text:
• Continuous equations or state integration
  • Direct scene-graph or physics mutation outside the command surface
  • A second implementation of a Modelica controller
  • Per-tick polling that should be an event

docs.title: A scenario is attached, not global
docs.text:
A scenario is a LunCoProgramAPI child prim, or a program started against a specific entity:

def Scope "Mission" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
) {
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover/scenarios/drive.rhai@
}

The asset source is loaded and hot-replaced by the asset layer. In the editor and API workflows you can also run a scenario directly against an entity with RunScenario, or run a file-backed asset with RunScenarioAsset.

docs.title: Lifecycle hooks
The command/query bridge
docs.text:
Scripts use the same public surface as the UI and HTTP API:

let result = cmd("SetPorts", #{ target: rover, writes: [["throttle", 0.4]] });
let state = query("QueryPhysicsState", #{ id: rover });
let rover = find("Rover");
  • cmd(name, params) performs a write with side effects.
  • query(name, params) reads state; no-data is (), failure is an error map.
  • emit(name, value) produces a telemetry event delivered to on_event.
  • Prelude helpers such as drive, brake, nav_to, possess, and input_hint compose common behavior.

The full command surface is generated by the running app and is intentionally larger than this page. Use the app's command reference or discover it over the HTTP API when you need an exact name.

docs.title: Events, not polling
docs.text: Production scenarios should react to events or task predicates. A fixed-tick on_tick loop is reserved for test sampling and verdicts. The kernel already advances tasks, waits, and event leaves; re-implementing that in a polling loop duplicates the runtime and makes the scenario less deterministic.

docs.title: Hot reload and teardown
docs.text:
Rhai is designed for a fast edit-run loop:

  • The native app loads the prelude and authored scripts from disk.
  • Editing a file-backed scenario can reload it without rebuilding Rust.
  • The outgoing program's on_stop runs before the new one starts.
  • On Twin close or scene replacement, the owner retires its scripts and state.

Always release control, stop actuators, and clear owned state in on_stop when the script acquired them.

docs.title: Determinism and ownership
docs.text:
Scenarios run in a defined owner scope and clock. Twin, application, and core policy are distinct. A script must not assume it can mutate another owner's state on an arbitrary thread.

Directives can select the execution target and timing:

// @peer host
// @timing simulation

host includes the standalone authoritative process. simulation is the default; presentation runs on application frames and may submit typed domain commands, but not direct structural world writes. Use these only when the behavior genuinely needs that scope.

docs.title: twin.toml
docs.text: twin.toml is the only file required for a folder to be a Twin. It identifies the project, selects the entry scene, and declares where the domain sources live. It does not contain physical equations or scene geometry.

docs.title: Minimal manifest
docs.text:
name = "my-rover-twin"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A minimal rover project"

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

The current format uses top-level name, version, and description. Unknown fields are rejected, so a typo fails visibly instead of being silently ignored.

docs.title: A fuller manifest
docs.text:
name = "Lunar Rover Lab"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Classroom practice project"

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"
scenes = ["scenes/*.usda", "scenes/tests/*.usda"]

[modelica]
paths = ["models"]
externals = [
  { name = "BundledModelicaLibraries", path = "@bundled:source-bundle" },
]

[sysml]
root = "requirements.sysml"
paths = ["."]

[settings]
"ui.lunar_map" = false

[[children]]
name = "engine"
path = "engine"

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning name Human-readable project name version Manifest/project version description Optional long description uuid Optional stable scenario identity used by networking default_perspective Optional authored initial task layout [usd].default_scene Twin-relative path to the stage opened when the Twin opens [usd].scenes Globs for scenes offered by the Scenarios menu [modelica].paths Twin-relative Modelica search roots; defaults to ["."] [modelica].externals Additional Modelica libraries, including @bundled:source-bundle [sysml].root Optional entry-point .sysml or .kerml file [sysml].paths Twin-relative SysML source roots; defaults to ["."] [settings] Scalar project settings read and written by Rhai policy [[children]] Nested Twins composed into this project [journal].persist Persist the edit journal across sessions; off by default

[[components]], [verification], and [[native_plugins]] are advanced project contracts. Most user Twins do not need them.

docs.title: How default_scene is chosen
docs.text:
The Twin does not guess a starting scene from a folder of .usda files. If default_scene is present, that exact Twin-relative stage becomes the active world when the Twin opens. If it is absent, the Twin opens like a folder: files are indexed, but no scene is auto-loaded.

Other .usda files in the Twin remain a referenceable library. Only the declared stage is mounted automatically. A scene can still reference them through normal USD composition.

[usd].scenes controls which files appear as loadable scenes in the Scenarios menu. If omitted, LunCoSim falls back to the conventional scenes/** and sim/scenes/** layouts. Declaring the globs explicitly is safer for a project that organizes scenes differently.

docs.title: Modelica and SysML roots
docs.text:
[modelica].paths tells the compiler where to look for .mo sources. A path may be "." to make the Twin root a search root. externals adds libraries outside the Twin, such as the bundled source library or a sibling folder.

[sysml] is optional. When present, root selects the entry-point source and paths narrows the source-set discovery. SysML files remain ordinary Twin files; the section does not embed model text or duplicate requirements.

docs.title: Twin settings
docs.text:
[settings] is a flat table of scalar values. Keys are namespaced strings:

[settings]
"ui.lunar_map" = false
"my_mission.max_speed" = 1.5

Rhai reads and writes them through get_twin_setting(...) and set_twin_setting(...). Use this for project policy and preferences, not for large structured data.

docs.title: Children and journal
docs.text:
[[children]] composes local child Twins. A child is opened as part of the parent, and a child can itself have a twin.toml.

[journal].persist = true writes the edit history to <twin>/history/journal.json. It is off by default; opening a folder should not start writing history into it unless the project asks for it.

docs.text:

docs.title: Twin
docs.text:
A Twin is a project folder for one engineered system: a lunar base, a rover test rig, a lander, a power subsystem, or a whole mission. It is the unit of saving, versioning, sharing, and opening in LunCoSim.

A folder becomes a Twin when it contains twin.toml. That manifest is the only required file.

docs.title: A minimal Twin
docs.text:
my-rover-twin/
├── twin.toml
├── scene.usda
├── models/
│   └── Drive.mo
├── scenarios/
│   └── drive.rhai
└── .lunco/              # session state, not project content

twin.toml declares the project name, version, entry scene, and search roots. The other files are ordinary domain files:

File Role scene.usda The USD scene that becomes the active world models/Drive.mo A Modelica source file scenarios/drive.rhai A Rhai scenario or test policy .lunco/ Local session and workspace state; normally gitignored

docs.title: Standard files, tool-specific manifest
docs.text:
A Twin deliberately separates tool configuration from system modeling:

  • USD owns geometry, composition, materials, physics, and connections.
  • Modelica owns equations and continuous state.
  • SysML owns requirements and system structure, when the Twin uses them.
  • Rhai owns scenario and test policy.
  • TOML owns tool configuration: twin.toml and Assets.toml.

The domain files stay in their standard syntax. A .mo file is still a normal Modelica file, a .usda file is still normal USD, and a .sysml file is still normal SysML. LunCoSim-specific configuration lives in twin.toml, so those files remain usable in other tools.

docs.title: File, folder, or Twin
docs.text:
LunCoSim supports three levels of structure:

Mode What you open What you get File One .usda, .mo, or other document Edit that file; no project-level discovery Folder A folder without twin.toml Browse and edit files; no manifest, no Twin search roots Twin A folder with twin.toml Full project discovery, default scene, libraries, and Twin settings

You can promote a folder to a Twin at any time by adding a twin.toml or by using Save as Twin…. The files do not move.

docs.title: Nested Twins
docs.text:
A Twin can compose child Twins:

[[children]]
name = "engine"
path = "engine"

Opening the parent loads local children eagerly. A child can be a complete project in its own right, which is useful for an engine, a comm stack, or a science payload that is also developed separately.

Remote URL children are reserved for future remote-Twin support; they are listed in the manifest but are not followed today.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Opening and closing a Twin is a real lifecycle boundary. When a Twin closes, its documents, Modelica participants, scripts, timelines, and scene-owned state are retired before another Twin can use those names. If you switch projects, expect a fresh load rather than a reuse of the previous session's state.

This is why a Twin is a better unit than a loose collection of tabs: the project owns its resources and can shut them down as one system.

docs.title: Create or open a Twin
docs.text:
• File → New Twin… creates a manifest and opens the new project.
  • File → Open Twin… opens an existing folder with twin.toml.
  • Save as Twin… promotes the current document or scene into a new project folder.

Once the Twin is open, the Twin panel shows its files. The declared default scene is loaded into the viewport; other USD files remain a referenceable asset library until a scene references them.

docs.title: USD
docs.text: OpenUSD is LunCoSim's scene and composition format. It describes what the world is made of: hierarchy, transforms, geometry, materials, physics schemas, and the typed connections between parts. It is not the physics engine and it is not a scripting language.

docs.title: What USD owns
docs.text:
• The prim hierarchy: assemblies, parts, mounts, sensors, and scene roots
  • Transforms and units
  • Mesh, curve, and primitive geometry
  • Materials and shader bindings
  • UsdPhysics rigid bodies, colliders, masses, and joints
  • Typed inputs: / outputs: ports and their connections
  • References, payloads, sublayers, and variants used for composition

docs.title: Units and orientation
docs.text:
A LunCoSim scene uses metres and a Y-up, right-handed world. A normal root stage declares that explicitly:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "MyTwin"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
)

def Xform "MyTwin" (kind = "assembly")
{
}

The defaultPrim matters: it gives the stage a stable root for references and for the runtime projection.

docs.title: Compose, do not duplicate
docs.text:
USD composition is how large scenes stay maintainable. A scene can reference a reusable rover, place two instances with different transforms, and select a variant without copying its geometry:

#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "PracticeYard"
    upAxis = "Y"
    metersPerUnit = 1
)

def Xform "PracticeYard"
{
    def Xform "RoverA" (
        prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 0, 0)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }

    def Xform "RoverB" (
        prepend references = @lunco://vessels/rovers/skid_rover.usda@
    )
    {
        double3 xformOp:translate = (8, 0, 4)
        uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
    }
}

lunco:// addresses the installed asset library. twin:// addresses a file in the open Twin. Use the narrowest authority that owns the file; do not escape an asset root with ...

docs.title: Physics is authored as SPD schemas
docs.text:
LunCoSim uses standard USD physics schemas rather than custom body objects. A movable part generally has:

  • a rigid body (UsdPhysics.RigidBodyAPI)
  • one or more colliders (UsdPhysics.CollisionAPI and a shape)
  • mass properties (UsdPhysics.MassAPI)
  • a joint when it is attached to another body

A movable mounted part needs both a rigid body and a joint. Being a child in the hierarchy is not an attachment. LunCoSim's scene linter reports a nested body without a joint.

docs.title: Programs are prims
docs.text:
A Modelica model or Rhai scenario is attached to a prim through the LunCoProgramAPI schema. The program is a child prim, so deleting the prim removes the behavior:

def Xform "Rover" (kind = "assembly")
{
    def Scope "Controller" (
        prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
    )
    {
        uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover/models/Drive.mo@
        uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true
    }
}

A shipped model uses @lunco://models/...@; a Twin-owned model uses @twin://...@. The source path is an asset address, not a relative path from the current working directory.

docs.title: Connections are USD facts
docs.text:
A connection is authored on the prim that consumes the value:

def Xform "DescentLander"
{
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @lunco://models/Lander.mo@
    uniform bool lunco:program:realtimeSafe = true

    float inputs:force_y.connect = </DescentLander.outputs:force_y>
    float inputs:q_w.connect = </DescentLander.outputs:quat_w>
}

The composed stage resolves references, payloads, variants, and the connection graph. The runtime then derives a SimConnection from the authored wire. A model output becomes externally connectable only when the component prim declares the matching outputs:<name> property; a connection target alone does not create a public port.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
Use the Build and Editor perspectives for normal authoring. The Editor opens one explicit USD document, previews changes, and saves through the document journal. The runtime does not rewrite authored USD to hide a bug. See Perspectives for the Editor layout and workflow.

The composed stage is inert. It becomes a live world only when the runtime projects it and the admitted programs start.

docs.title: First lesson
docs.text: The first lesson is a real simulation, not a slideshow. You take control of a rover, drive it with physics, and complete objectives that are checked against the live world.

docs.title: Option A — Lunar Rover Lab (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Tutorials → Start Here → Lunar Rover Lab

This is the recommended classroom activity. You will:

  1. Drive to a marker and stop inside it.
  2. Open a speed graph and identify a real motion sample.
  3. Predict the result of changing drive demand, then run two trials.
  4. Explain the measured result.
  5. Move a block into an authoring bay.
  6. Save the result as your own Twin.

The lesson card stays visible across perspectives. Instructor checkpoints let you jump to driving, telemetry, or comparison practice without pretending the earlier tasks were completed. Restart whole lab (discard edits) resets the document through the normal scene restart.

docs.title: Option B — First Drive (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Tutorials → Sandbox → First Drive

Use this when you only want to see the core loop:

  1. Open the lesson.
  2. Click Take control.
  3. Drive to the glowing flag.
  4. Stop inside the marker.

The rover's motion comes from the authored Modelica controller and the native physics engine. The lesson script observes possession, the flag sensor, and the rover's speed; it does not advance from elapsed time.

The lesson card names the current objective and the actions that are valid now. Progress is checked against the live simulation.

docs.title: Reading the lesson card
docs.text:
The card shows the current objective and the actions that are valid now. Some actions are mouse buttons in the card, some are keyboard controls, and some are buttons that open another perspective.

The lesson uses semantic input hints such as forward, brake, and left. The displayed key is resolved from your current input bindings, so re-binding an action changes both the actual control and the lesson text. See Controls.

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
Under the lesson there is a normal Twin:

  • A USD scene owns the rover, the ground, the flag, the camera, and the sensors.
  • A Modelica model owns the rover's continuous drive behavior.
  • A Rhai scenario owns the lesson steps, hints, objectives, and completion checks.
  • The runtime projects the scene into physics, steps the model, and delivers events back to the scenario.

That division is the main idea behind LunCoSim. Continue with How it fits together.

docs.title: First run
docs.text: When LunCoSim opens, you are looking at a workbench, not a single fixed editor. The same Twin can be viewed as a running mission, a scene assembly, a graph dashboard, a USD document, or a Modelica model.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
Area What it does Title bar Documentation, Community, Tutorials, and the perspective tabs Viewport The live 3D scene, selection, camera, and ground interaction Side panels Twin files, Entity tree, Inspector, Environment, Spawn, Telemetry, Ports Bottom dock Graphs, timelines, logs, and document tabs Status bar Update notices, simulation state, and transient messages

The exact panels depend on the active perspective. View → Reset Layout restores the authored default for the current task.

The View perspective with the First Drive sandbox open. Panels and tabs change when you switch perspectives.

docs.title: Perspectives
docs.text:
Choose a perspective from the title bar or View → Perspectives:

Perspective Use it for View Operating the live mission in a full-window scene Build Composing the scene from assemblies, entities, and the Twin's files Analyze Comparing signals in Graphs, with Telemetry and Ports Editor Editing one explicit USD document in an isolated preview Lunica Modelica diagrams, equations, compilation, and experiments

Switching perspectives preserves the Twin and the simulation. You are changing the layout and the visible tools, not restarting the world.

For a detailed tour of each task and its controls, see Perspectives.

docs.title: Open the Tutorials menu
docs.text:
The Tutorials menu contains the authored lesson catalog. Tracks include Start Here, LunCoSim, Navigation, Sandbox, Rover Driving, and Modelica.

Each entry is a tour, an exercise, or a challenge:

  • A tour explains where things are. It does not certify that you performed an action.
  • An exercise advances only when the simulation observes the requested result.
  • A challenge is a longer open-ended task.

Selecting a lesson loads its authored scene when the lesson needs one, then starts the lesson's Rhai scenario. This is the easiest way to see a working Twin without building one first.

docs.title: First five minutes
docs.text:
1. Open Tutorials → Start Here → Lunar Rover Lab for the full 30-minute classroom exercise, or Tutorials → Sandbox → First Drive for a five-minute rover drive.
  2. Wait for the scene and the lesson card to settle. The viewport shows the practice yard; the card explains the current step.
  3. Click Take control. Selection is not control: you must claim the rover before your input reaches it.
  4. Drive with the displayed bindings. The defaults are W/S for forward and reverse, A/D to steer, and Space to brake. The lesson uses input_hint(...), so it always shows the bindings currently configured on your machine.
  5. Follow the on-screen objective. When you reach the marker, stop inside it. The lesson checks the simulation state, not a timer.

If the rover rolls over, use Right rover. If you lose the view, use Return camera. Both actions preserve lesson progress.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text:
• The vehicle ignores your input: click Take control first.
  • The viewport is empty: open a scene or lesson; a Twin with no default_scene opens as a file browser, not a world.
  • An asset is missing: LunCoSim asks before downloading declared external assets. See Assets.toml.
  • The app will not start on a port: choose another free --api port.

Continue with First lesson for the suggested learning path, or read How it fits together to understand what the lesson is doing behind the scenes.

docs.title: Install LunCoSim
docs.text: The supported way to use LunCoSim is the packaged desktop application. Build from source only if you are developing the engine.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
Get the current installer from the LunCoSim releases page.

Platform Package Launch Windows x86_64 LunCoSim-Windows-x86_64-Setup.exe Start-menu or desktop shortcut macOS Apple Silicon LunCoSim-macOS-Apple-Silicon.pkg Installed LunCoSim.app macOS Intel LunCoSim-macOS-Intel.pkg Installed LunCoSim.app Linux x86_64 LunCoSim-Linux-x86_64.AppImage The same AppImage from a writable location

Do not launch Setup.exe again to use the app, and do not launch a copied .app binary or a source-build executable if you want the updater to work. Use the installed shortcut or the same AppImage you originally placed on disk.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Run LunCoSim-Windows-x86_64-Setup.exe and follow the installer. Launch LunCoSim from the Start menu or the desktop shortcut.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: Open the .pkg and install LunCoSim.app where the installer offers. Launch the installed application from Finder or Launchpad.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
The Linux package is an AppImage. Place it somewhere writable, make it executable, and run it:

chmod +x LunCoSim-Linux-x86_64.AppImage
./LunCoSim-Linux-x86_64.AppImage

There is no system-wide installation step. Keep the AppImage in a location where you can replace it, because the built-in updater replaces that file.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
LunCoSim may check the release feed once at startup. If an update is available, the status bar shows a clickable notice. Choose Download update, then Install and restart when the package is ready.

The application is ready when the main window shows the 3D viewport and the perspective tabs. Continue with First run.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text: Source builds are for contributors and for running the newest unreleased code. Packaged users do not need Rust or LLVM.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Rust toolchain selected by the repository (rust-toolchain.toml)
  • LLVM/libclang for the FMI import dependency
  • The native windowing and audio development libraries used by Bevy

On Debian/Ubuntu, the CI build installs:

sudo apt-get install -y \
  libasound2-dev libudev-dev \
  libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev \
  libx11-dev xorg-dev

On macOS, the Xcode Command Line Tools provide libclang. On Windows, install the MSVC C++ Build Tools and Windows SDK, then install LLVM:

winget install --exact --id LLVM.LLVM --architecture x64

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/LunCoSim/lunco-sim.git
cd lunco-sim
cargo build -p lunco-luncosim --bin luncosim -j 4
target/debug/luncosim --api 4101

Run from the repository root so the application can find its bundled assets. The --api flag is optional, but an explicit free port is useful for scripts, screenshots, and inspection. Do not reuse a port that another LunCoSim session is already using.

If the build reports Unable to find libclang, verify that LLVM contains libclang and that LIBCLANG_PATH points to its containing directory if it is not in the default location.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• First run — the window, perspectives, and where to click
  • First lesson — a five-minute rover exercise

docs.title: Perspectives
docs.text:
A perspective is a task layout over the same Twin. Switching from View to Build, Analyze, Editor, or Lunica does not reload the scene, reset the simulation, or duplicate your project. It changes which tools are docked and what the center of the window is for.

The title bar pins the five main tasks. View → Perspectives lists every available task, including specialist presets such as Terrain.

Perspective Task View Observe and operate the running Twin Analyze Inspect and compare simulation signals Build Compose the live scene Editor Edit one explicitly opened USD document Lunica Edit, compile, and run Modelica models

Analyze is the built-in label for analytics work; there is no separate Analytics tab.

docs.title: Switch and recover a layout
docs.text:
Select a title-bar tab, or choose View → Perspectives and pick a task. Compact windows collapse the tabs into a picker. Switching perspectives preserves the Twin and the simulation; layout changes stay with their task.

  • View → Reset Layout reapplies the authored default for the current perspective.
  • Help → Perspective help explains what the current perspective is for.
  • The View menu also has task submenus (Build, Analyze, Editor, Lunica, and General) that open optional panels.
  • The Graphs menu action switches to Analyze when that workflow is available.

A guided lesson can temporarily pin the perspective its steps rely on. When the lesson completes or is skipped, normal perspective switching resumes.

docs.title: View: operate the mission
docs.text:
View gives the live scene the whole window. It is the perspective to use when the task is to watch, drive, fly, or demonstrate rather than author.

The viewport keeps selection, control, and camera targets separate. Selecting an object does not give you its controls, and moving the camera does not change what is selected.

The View perspective leaves the live scene full-window. Open optional panels from View when you need them.

To use it:

  1. Open a scene or lesson and let the scene finish preparing.
  2. Click an object to select it, or click an input endpoint to take control of a vehicle or mechanism. In a lesson, use the Take control action when the card offers it.
  3. Drive with the displayed bindings. The lesson card and the active input map always show the keys configured on your machine.
  4. Right-drag to orbit and scroll to zoom. The camera keeps its own target.
  5. Use the transport controls or P to pause when you need to inspect a moment without stopping the app.

Use View for operating and presenting a Twin. Switch to Build when you need to add or edit scene objects, and to Analyze when you need the signal data behind what you see.

docs.title: Analyze: read the signals
docs.text:
Analyze is the telemetry and plotting perspective. The live scene remains in the center, Telemetry sits above Entities on the left, Ports is on the right, and Graphs occupies the bottom dock.

Analyze brings the live scene, Telemetry, Ports, and Graphs together. Graphs records simulation samples, not rendered frames.

To compare signals:

  1. Switch to Analyze. If no scene is mounted, Graphs opens in the center.
  2. Select an entity in Entities, or choose it in Telemetry, to narrow the channel list.
  3. Check a channel, or drag it into the active plot in Graphs. Add more channels to the same plot to compare them on one time axis.
  4. Use Ports to read current values and to write manual inputs while the model is running. Use the port's direction and kind: write inputs, read outputs.
  5. Pause the simulation to inspect the latest sample. The graph keeps the samples it already recorded; it does not replay rendered frames.

If Graphs is hidden, use the Graphs menu or open the optional View → Analyze panels. Graphs is the canonical analysis surface; the same data is also available through the HTTP API when you need to script a check.

docs.title: Build: compose the live scene
docs.text:
Build is the scene-composition perspective. Entities sits above the Twin file browser on the left, the live scene is in the center, and Inspector and Environment sit above the Spawn palette on the right.

Build places the scene tree, Twin files, Inspector, Environment, and Spawn palette around the live scene.

To assemble a scene:

  1. Open the Twin or scene you want to edit. Build edits the live scene, so the simulation keeps running while you work.
  2. Select an object in Entities to inspect it, or choose an assembly in the Spawn palette.
  3. Place the new object, then adjust its transform and properties in Inspector or with the viewport transform gizmo.
  4. Use Environment for scene-wide settings such as lighting and the environment profile.
  5. Save the scene document to keep the change in the authored USD stage.

Build is for composing the world from assemblies and entities. When you need to edit the internals of a reusable assembly, open that USD document in Editor. When you need the signal behind a behavior, use Analyze.

docs.title: Editor: edit one USD document
docs.text:
Editor is a focused USD authoring perspective. Twin and Prims are on the left, the document preview is in the center, and Inspector, Requirements, and Change History are on the right. The center stays empty until you open a document or tool.

Editor opens one USD document in an isolated preview. Selecting a prim drives the Inspector; save and undo apply to that document.

To edit a document:

  1. Choose a USD file in Twin, or use File → Open. The file opens as an editing preview; it does not replace the live scene.
  2. Select a prim in Prims or click it in the preview. The Inspector shows the selected prim's properties.
  3. Edit the value in the Inspector, or switch between Visual and Text to inspect the rendered stage or its USD text.
  4. Left-drag to pan, right-drag to orbit, middle-drag to pan, and use the wheel to zoom. The transform gizmo edits the selected prim directly.
  5. Review the journal in Change History. Save and Undo apply to the active document, not to the live scene.

Opening a scene through Scenarios is a world load; opening a USD file in Editor is a document edit. To find a prim's file in the Twin browser, right-click the prim and choose Reveal in Twin.

Editor is the right place for reusable assembly internals, prim hierarchy, materials, and authored properties. It deliberately does not show the live Entity list or Spawn palette; use Build for the composed world.

docs.title: Lunica: engineer a Modelica model
docs.text:
Lunica is the Modelica perspective. The Twin browser is on the left, and the center holds the Welcome page or the model views you open. Models open in their own document tabs; inside a model, switch between Text, Diagram, Icon, and Docs.

Lunica opens Modelica sources from the Twin. Compile the model, run it live, or use Fast Run for a batch experiment.

To work on a model:

  1. Switch to Lunica, then choose the Modelica view in the Twin browser to browse packages and classes. Open a .mo file to create a model tab.
  2. Work in Diagram for the schematic, or Text for the equations.
  3. Choose Compile to build the model. A successful compile leaves the model ready and paused.
  4. Choose Run to start live simulation, then pause, reset, or restart from the same toolbar. Use Fast Run when you want a batch run that does not need to play in real time.
  5. Open View → Lunica → Experiments to revisit completed runs and compare their variables. For signals from the running Twin, use Analyze instead.

Lunica edits and runs Modelica; it does not replace the USD scene or the Rhai scenario. Use it to develop the continuous model, then wire that model into the Twin and observe the coupled behavior in Analyze or View.

docs.title: Choose the right task
docs.text:
You want to… Use Drive, fly, or present the running mission View Compare telemetry and inspect current port values Analyze Add, place, or tune objects in the live scene Build Edit the prims and properties inside a USD document Editor Develop, compile, and run a Modelica model Lunica

Additional task presets, such as Terrain, appear under View → Perspectives but are not pinned to the title bar. A Twin can also add its own perspectives; they appear beside the built-in tasks.

Switching perspectives is part of normal work, not a reset. If a layout feels wrong, use View → Reset Layout for the current task, or open Help → Perspective help to confirm what that task is meant to do.

Continue with First lesson for a guided flow. For the full keyboard and camera reference, see Controls.

docs.title: Create a Twin
docs.text:
There are two practical ways to start a project:

  • Promote a working scene. Open a lesson or example, then save it as a new Twin. This is the fastest way to get a real scene with physics, models, and scripts.
  • Start empty. Create a new Twin and add your own scene and sources.

docs.title: Promote a scene into a Twin
docs.text:
1. Launch LunCoSim.
  2. Open Tutorials → Sandbox → First Drive so a working scene is mounted.
  3. Choose File → Save as Twin….
  4. Select or create an empty folder for the project.
  5. Confirm. LunCoSim writes twin.toml and opens the new Twin.

The new folder contains the scene document and the manifest. The scene keeps its normal lunco:// references to the installed library; it is a project that uses the shared asset bundle, not a self-contained copy of every referenced asset.

The Build perspective keeps the scene tree, the Twin's files, the Inspector, and the Spawn palette together while the simulation keeps running.

docs.title: Start from a new Twin
docs.text:
Choose File → New Twin…, select a folder, and provide a name. LunCoSim creates the manifest and opens the project. You can add a scene later.

A minimal manifest looks like this:

name = "my-rover-twin"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "My first LunCoSim project"

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

The folder should look like:

my-rover-twin/
├── twin.toml
├── scene.usda
├── models/
│   └── Drive.mo
├── scenarios/
│   └── drive.rhai
└── .lunco/

default_scene is the important line. It tells LunCoSim which USD stage becomes the active world when the Twin opens. Without it, the Twin opens as a file browser and does not mount a scene.

docs.title: Add behavior
docs.text:
• Modelica goes in .mo files under the Twin, then a USD LunCoProgramAPI prim points at it with info:sourceAsset.
  • Rhai goes in .rhai files under the Twin, then a LunCoProgramAPI prim points at the scenario.
  • External assets go in Assets.toml, never as hardcoded cache paths.

The next guide builds a scenario:

Write a Rhai scenario

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Open the Twin and choose its default scene, or load the scene directly:

luncosim --api 4101 --scene /path/to/my-rover-twin/scene.usda

Use an explicit free API port. Run from the folder containing the Twin if you are using a source build and relative asset paths.

docs.title: Check the manifest
docs.text:
If the Twin does not open the scene you expect:

  1. Confirm default_scene is a path relative to the Twin root.
  2. Confirm the file exists and is a valid .usda.
  3. Reopen the Twin after editing the manifest; the manifest is read at open.
  4. Check that unknown fields are not present — the manifest parser rejects typos.

See twin.toml for the field reference.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
LunCoSim exposes a small HTTP API for automation, inspection, tests, and screenshots. It is the same typed command/query surface used by the UI and by Rhai, not a second control path.

Launch with an explicit free port:

luncosim --api 4101

The command endpoint is loopback-only. Do not expose it to an untrusted network.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Method Path Purpose POST /api/commands Execute a command or query GET /api/commands/schema Discover command names and field types GET /api/health Liveness; does not read the world GET /api/ready Readiness, scene hold, and pending work GET /api/diagnostics Co-simulation wiring and connection health

docs.title: Request envelope
docs.text:
Every write and query uses the same JSON envelope:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "type": "ExecuteCommand",
        "command": "SetPorts",
        "params": {
          "target": 42,
          "producer_id": 4812,
          "writes": [["throttle", 0.4], ["steer", 0.0], ["brake", 0.0]],
          "seq": 0,
          "tick": 0
        }
      }'

The successful response wraps the owner's result:

{
  "data": {
    "accepted": true
  }
}

An error response is terminal. Do not retry a rejected command blindly; read the error, inspect the target, and fix the input.

ListEntities can also be sent as a shorthand request:

{"type": "ListEntities"}

docs.title: Discover the surface
docs.text:
Never guess a command name from memory:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands/schema" | python3 -m json.tool

The schema is derived from the running application's reflected command and query types. It grows with the features actually registered in that build.

docs.title: Readiness
docs.text:
Before controlling a scene, wait for readiness:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/ready"

Continue only when ready is true, world_hold is false, and pending_count is zero. A faulted world is not a slow world; inspect the readiness detail and /api/diagnostics.

docs.title: Commands and queries
docs.text:
The API has both write commands and read queries. They share ExecuteCommand for transport, but their contract differs:

  • A write command has side effects and returns an acceptance/result.
  • A query reads state and returns typed data.
  • A rejected command does not partially apply a multi-target write.
  • A missing value is not silently replaced with a zero.

Common discovery/read examples:

# Entities, including their stable api_id
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ListEntities"}'

# Ports on one entity
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "ListPorts",
       "params": {"api_id": 42}}'

docs.title: Driving from a script
docs.text:
A Python or shell client only needs an HTTP request. There is no SDK and no handshake:

import json
import urllib.request

def execute(command, params=None):
    body = json.dumps({
        "type": "ExecuteCommand",
        "command": command,
        "params": params or {},
    }).encode()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        "http://127.0.0.1:4101/api/commands",
        data=body,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
        payload = json.load(response)
    if "error" in payload:
        raise RuntimeError(payload["error"])
    return payload["data"]

entities = execute("ListEntities")["entities"]

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
• The API is a transport. Domain state is still owned by USD, Modelica, Rhai, and the native runtime.
  • Use LoadScene, not direct file writes, to mount a scene.
  • Use SetPorts for a live input hold; use ReleaseControl or ReleasePort to return the input to its authored source.
  • Use CaptureScreenshot for visual evidence; do not infer a rendered result from a numeric query alone.
  • Run scene tests through the production binary (luncosim test), not through a private HTTP loop that skips the authored verdict.

For live values, see Inspect telemetry. For command-line flags, see CLI.

docs.title: Inspect telemetry
docs.text: Telemetry is a first-class runtime surface. Read it from the Analyze perspective or from the HTTP API; do not tail a log or poll a screenshot for a number.

docs.title: In the window
docs.text:
1. Switch to Analyze.
  2. Open Telemetry. It lists the live port-bearing entities and their channels.
  3. Select an entity to see its current values. An absent port is not a zero; the entity may still be preparing.
  4. Open Graphs and add a channel to see it over time. This is the right tool for settling, oscillation, and arrival checks.
  5. Use Ports to inspect the resolved direction and kind of each port before wiring a target.

The graph records real simulation samples. It is not a render-frame animation. When the world is paused, the last sample stays visible.

The Analyze perspective brings Telemetry, Ports, and Graphs together. Select a channel in Telemetry to plot its samples in Graphs.

docs.title: From the HTTP API
docs.text:
Start LunCoSim with an explicit port:

luncosim --api 4101

Find an entity:

PORT=4101

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ListEntities"}'

The response contains each entity's api_id. Use that identity for reads:

# Discover the port names first; ReadPorts requires explicit names.
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "ListPorts",
       "params": {"api_id": 42}}'

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "ReadPorts",
       "params": {"api_id": 42,
                  "port_names": ["throttle", "steer", "speed"]}}'

ReadPorts returns one shared sim_tick and the selected rows. It does not dump every port on an entity; name what you need. Use ReadPortsBatch when you need the same sample across several entities.

docs.title: Modelica state
docs.text:
A rendered port is not necessarily the whole solver state. To inspect the Modelica side:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "SnapshotVariables",
       "params": {"api_id": 42}}'

SnapshotVariables answers "what does the model currently hold?" Use ReadPorts for "what is exposed at the wiring boundary?" and CosimStatus for the end-to-end Modelica → physics chain.

docs.title: Readiness matters
docs.text:
Before treating a value as final, check readiness:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/ready"

Require:

  • ready: true
  • world_hold: false
  • pending_count: 0

A port may be momentarily absent while its model is compiling or its scene is still being admitted. That is different from a valid zero.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Numbers answer "what value?" A screenshot answers "does the scene look right?" Capture the visible production window, not a headless substitute:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/api/commands" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "ExecuteCommand", "command": "CaptureScreenshot",
       "params": {"save_to_file": true, "path": "target/telemetry-check.png"}}'

The path is relative to the process working directory. Read the resulting PNG before reporting a visual result.

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text:
Trap Better read Polling stdout for a value ReadPorts or the Telemetry panel Treating a missing port as 0.0 Check readiness and ListPorts Using a single sample for a trend Record a graph or a time series Reading a render FPS as simulation cadence Inspect the clock and timing profile Comparing values from different ticks Use one ReadPorts/ReadPortsBatch response Looking only at ports for solver state Also call SnapshotVariables

See HTTP API for the request envelope and the discovery endpoint.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with the visible owner: the status bar, the lesson card, the readiness endpoint, or the terminal that launched the app. A log line is evidence only when it names the same failure.

docs.title: The app does not start
docs.text:
--api port is already in use

Choose a different free port:

luncosim --api 4102

Do not reuse a port owned by another LunCoSim session. Stop only your own session through its API, then relaunch.

The window does not appear

Check that the machine has a working display and GPU driver. For a headless or remote run, use the documented headless/recording options rather than expecting a window.

A source build fails on libclang

Install LLVM. On Windows:

winget install --exact --id LLVM.LLVM --architecture x64

On Debian/Ubuntu, install libclang-dev or the matching LLVM package. If libclang is not in a default location, set LIBCLANG_PATH to the directory that contains it.

Linux build fails on a missing system library

Install the windowing and audio development headers:

sudo apt-get install -y \
  libasound2-dev libudev-dev \
  libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev \
  libx11-dev xorg-dev

docs.title: The scene is empty or the Twin opens as files
docs.text:
A Twin only mounts a scene when twin.toml declares it:

[usd]
default_scene = "scene.usda"

The path is relative to the Twin root. If it is missing or wrong, the Twin opens as a file browser. Check that the file exists and that the manifest has no unknown-field typo; the parser rejects unknown fields.

If the scene loads but the ground is missing, a terrain asset is probably not installed. See Assets below.

docs.title: The vehicle ignores input
docs.text:
1. Click Take control or use possess. Selection is not control.
  2. Confirm the vehicle is not held by another session or producer.
  3. Check that the input binding is actually mapped. The lesson hint resolves the current binding; a label of unbound means the action has no key.
  4. If a script holds the vehicle, release that claim before taking manual control.

docs.title: An asset is missing
docs.text:
LunCoSim does not download external data silently at launch. When a declared asset is missing:

  1. Open Settings → Data & libraries or the Twin's assets view.
  2. Confirm the entry exists in Assets.toml with a valid url and dest.
  3. Start the download explicitly and watch its status.
  4. If a hash is declared, a mismatch rejects the download. Remove the bad cache artifact only after confirming the source, then retry.

The cache lives at:

Platform Path Linux ~/.cache/lunco/ macOS ~/Library/Caches/lunco/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\lunco\

Set LUNCOSIM_CACHE to use a different root. Do not hardcode a cache path in a USD file; use lunco:// or twin:// addresses instead.

docs.title: The rover does not move
docs.text:
Check the whole chain, not just the script:

  1. Does the scenario attach to the entity that should act?
  2. Does the drive model compile and report a running participant?
  3. Does the component declare the outputs: port that the connection targets?
  4. Is the target input actually wired to a source?
  5. Is a higher-priority control hold keeping the input at another value?

A missing port is not a zero. Inspect it with ListPorts and the wiring diagnostics rather than assuming a default.

docs.title: Modelica does not run
docs.text:
• Check that the .mo file parses and compiles in the Lunica perspective.
  • Confirm the Twin's [modelica].paths includes the model's root.
  • Confirm the USD program prim names the exact source asset.
  • Check that required external libraries are installed and declared.
  • Read the participant status and cosim diagnostics; a model that stopped is not a model that is still advancing.

docs.title: Telemetry shows no value
docs.text:
• Wait for readiness; a port can be absent while its model is compiling.
  • Run ListPorts before ReadPorts; reads require explicit port names.
  • For solver state, use SnapshotVariables, not only the port surface.
  • If a value was valid earlier and then vanished, check whether the owning entity or scene was replaced.

docs.title: The API rejects a request
docs.text:
• Read the error. Unknown fields and malformed nested values are rejected, not ignored.
  • Confirm the command name with GET /api/commands/schema.
  • Confirm IDs are the stable api_id, not a display name or a local index.
  • For a multi-target write, fix the whole batch; a rejection means no partial writes were admitted.
  • Do not retry a rejected input with the same value and expect a different result.

docs.title: The updater says NotInstalled
docs.text:
Automatic updates only work from a supported installed package:

  • the Windows Setup.exe installation
  • the installed macOS app
  • the same Linux AppImage you originally launched

A source build and an ordinary extracted archive correctly report NotInstalled. Reinstall from the current release to restore update support.

docs.title: What to include in a report
docs.text:
Include:

  • the LunCoSim version and platform
  • whether it is a packaged build or a source build
  • the exact scene or Twin path
  • the exact command or input that failed
  • the readiness/diagnostic response
  • a screenshot when the failure is visual
  • the first error, not only the last log line

Never include secrets, tokens, or private asset URLs in a public report.

docs.title: Write a Rhai scenario
docs.text: A scenario is an ordinary .rhai file attached to an entity. This guide builds a small mission that drives a rover to a marker, reports arrival, and shows an objective on the HUD.

docs.title: 1. Create the file
docs.text:
Add a scenario inside your Twin:

my-rover-twin/
└── scenarios/
    └── drive.rhai

docs.title: 2. Write the policy
docs.text:
fn marker() {
    [12.0, 0.0, 8.0]
}

fn task(me, ctx) {
    let goal = marker();
    seq([
        once(|m| notify("Driving to the marker")),
        step(|m| nav_to(m, goal, 1.2, 2.0),
             |m| arrived(m, goal, 2.0)),
        once(|m| {
            brake(m);
            emit("MARKER_REACHED", goal);
        }),
    ])
}

fn mission(me, ctx) {
    let goal = marker();
    [
        objective("reach_marker", #{
            text: "Drive to the marker",
            done: |m| arrived(m, goal, 2.0),
        }),
    ]
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "MARKER_REACHED" {
        notify_kind("Marker reached", "success");
    }
}

What each part does:

Part Role task(me, ctx) Returns a task tree that the native behavior kernel advances seq([...]) Runs steps in order once(...) Runs one action and advances step(act, done) Repeats act until done is true, then advances wait(secs) Suspends for simulation seconds wait_until(pred) Suspends until the predicate becomes true wait_for("NAME") Suspends until a named event arrives mission(me, ctx) Declares objectives checked against live state on_event(...) Reacts to an event outside the task tree

nav_to is a prelude helper that publishes a waypoint to the authored drive law. It does not integrate motion itself. arrived reads the authoritative pose and checks the radius.

Do not add on_tick to a production scenario. The task kernel already advances steps, waits, and predicates; a hand-written tick loop duplicates it and makes the scenario less deterministic. on_tick is reserved for test sampling.

docs.title: 3. Attach the scenario
docs.text:
A scenario is not global. Attach it to the entity that owns the behavior, or to a dedicated mission-control entity that never moves:

def Scope "Mission" (
    prepend apiSchemas = ["LunCoProgramAPI"]
) {
    uniform asset info:sourceAsset = @twin://my-rover-twin/scenarios/drive.rhai@
}

Place this prim under the entity that should be me. Use @twin://...@ for a file in the open Twin. The scenario must still find its target by name or by an explicit reference; attachment does not automatically pick a rover.

docs.title: 4. Run and iterate
docs.text:
Open the Twin and load its default scene. The scenario starts when the scene is admitted. To iterate:

  • Edit the .rhai file; the asset watcher hot-reloads a file-backed scenario.
  • The old instance's on_stop runs before the new one starts.
  • Use Restart scene if you changed USD structure rather than script logic.
  • Use Scenarios to load a different declared scene.

If you need to start a scenario explicitly, use RunScenario or RunScenarioAsset from the API or another script. A UI-only scenario can pass an empty scene asset.

docs.title: 5. Observe events
docs.text:
Events are the preferred coordination mechanism:

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name == "MARKER_REACHED" {
        this.reached = true;
    }
    if evt.name == "LOW_FUEL" {
        notify_kind("Fuel is low", "warn");
    }
}

A script emits with emit("NAME", value). Events are delivered on the next fixed step, so ordering does not depend on entity iteration order. Scenarios do not call each other directly; they interact through the event bus and the shared command/query surface.

docs.title: 6. Add a verdict
docs.text:
A scenario can also be a test. Use the prelude assertions and report one typed verdict at the end:

fn on_start(me, ctx) {
    this.start = world_pos3(me);
    this.reported = false;
}

fn on_event(me, evt, ctx) {
    if evt.name != "MARKER_REACHED" { return; }
    if this.reported { return; }
    this.reported = true;

    let pos = world_pos3(me);
    let distance = if pos == () || this.start == () {
        ()
    } else {
        vlen(vsub(pos, this.start))
    };

    let fails = [];
    fails.push(t_present(pos, "rover position"));
    fails.push(t_moved(distance, 3.0, "rover travel"));
    report_verdict(fails, "DRIVE TEST", "DRIVE_TEST");
}

t_moved uses the measured distance, not a hardcoded pass value. Pairing it with t_present also proves the test read a real position. Run the scenario through the production scene-test binary, not a private harness.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Nothing moves nav_to has no authored steering capability, so it brakes safely Rover ignores the script The scenario is attached to the wrong entity, or a session holds manual control Objective never completes done reads a stale or missing owner value Event handler never runs The event name differs, or the scenario was replaced before delivery Hot reload does nothing The script was started from an inline source, not a file-backed asset

Next: Inspect telemetry to read the values your scenario produces.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The luncosim binary can open the desktop app, serve the API headlessly, run a scene test, validate assets, or connect the Rhai REPL to a running session.

luncosim [FLAGS]
luncosim rhai [--api PORT] [-e SNIPPET | -f FILE]
luncosim test --scene PATH
luncosim --validate PATH…

Run luncosim --help for the help text of the installed version.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
Flag Meaning --scene PATH Load this USD scene at startup. The path may be relative to assets/, to the current directory, or absolute --api [PORT] Serve the HTTP command API on the given port --no-ui Run headless, without a window. Also LUNCO_NO_UI=1 --window-pos SPEC Place the window, for example 1920x1080+0+0 --validate PATH… Parse-check asset files and exit without opening a window or GPU

--no-ui does not imply --api. Pass both when a headless run needs the API:

luncosim --no-ui --api 4101 --scene scenes/tests/rover.usda

Without --scene, the app starts with an empty persistent world shell. The sandbox is an explicit scene or lesson, not an implicit startup default.

docs.title: Recording and capture
docs.text:
Flag Meaning --record-offline <dir|out.mp4> Record deterministic frames. A directory receives a PNG sequence; a video path streams to ffmpeg --record-fps N Output frame rate; default 60 --record-preset MODE H.264 preset; default ultrafast --record-frames N Stop after N frames --offscreen Render windowlessly into an offscreen target and exit when the take drains --record-size WxH Offscreen target resolution; default 1280x720

A one-command windowless take:

luncosim --offscreen --scene scenes/demo.usda \
  --record-offline /tmp/demo.mp4 --record-frames 300

Recording is deterministic once the scene is ready. Do not judge render cost from a recording run; use a separate profiling session.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Flag Meaning --host [PORT] Host a WebTransport session; default port 5888 --connect ADDR Join a hosted session; a missing port implies port 5888 --cert PATH TLS certificate: a certbot live directory or a certificate file --key PATH TLS private key when --cert names a file

Omit --cert and --key for a development self-signed certificate. A bare IP address for --connect skips TLS validation for a LAN/development run.

Networking is opt-in at build time. A default local build does not start a multiplayer host.

docs.title: Rendering and performance
docs.text:
Flag Meaning --render-profile MODE standard preserves authored PBR; fast uses unlit, texture-free materials and disables HDR, bloom, and MSAA --render-quality MODE low, balanced, or high graphics budgets --no-vsync Uncap the frame rate --no-throttle Keep running at full rate while unfocused --headless-max-speed With --no-ui, advance the fixed simulation lattice as fast as the CPU and causal participants allow --log-diag Log FPS, frame-time, and physics diagnostics --console Windows: enable the debug console for this launch

--render-quality changes GPU budgets; it does not replace the shaders authored by the scene. When measuring FPS, use --no-vsync --no-throttle so you are not timing the compositor or the unfocused power-save throttle.

docs.title: Rhai REPL
docs.text:
Connect to a running instance's API port:

luncosim rhai --api 4101
luncosim rhai --api 4101 -e 'print(find("Rover"))'
luncosim rhai --api 4101 -f scripts/check.rhai

The REPL evaluates against the live app. It is useful for inspection and small commands; authored tests belong in a scene test.

docs.title: Scene tests
docs.text:
luncosim test --scene assets/scenes/tests/rover_drive.usda

A scene test runs the authored Rhai test headlessly and deterministically. The exit code is the verdict:

Exit Meaning 0 PASS 1 FAIL 2 No verdict was produced

Use --verdict-channel NAME to select a specific typed verdict channel. Use --verification KEY with a Twin-owned SysML verification registry entry to run that requirement's authored check.

Do not use a private test harness or --validate as a substitute for runtime behavior. --validate only proves that the files parse and their declarations are structurally valid.

docs.title: Asset validation
docs.text:
luncosim --validate path/to/model.mo path/to/scene.usda

Supported inputs include .mo, .usda, .sysml, .kerml, .wesl, and .rhai. The command is parse-only: no window, GPU, or app launch. It exits 0 when every input is valid and 1 when any input fails.

docs.text:

  • HTTP API — command and query envelope
  • Install — packaged and source builds

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: These are the shipped default bindings. Tutorials and lessons show the current binding through input_hint(...), so rebinding an action updates both the control and the on-screen hint.

docs.title: Movement
docs.text:
Action Default Forward W Backward S Left A Right D Yaw left Q Yaw right E Speed boost Shift

The same movement set applies to walking and to driving. A vehicle first needs to be possessed; selection alone does not send input to it.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Action Default Context action F Thrust / brake Space Release G Switch mode V Pause P Cancel Backspace or Escape Delete selection Delete

Space is both thrust and brake depending on the controlled vehicle and mode. The active control mode decides which effect applies.

docs.title: Camera and selection
docs.text:
Action Default Look / orbit Hold right mouse button and move Select Left click Extend selection Shift + left click Remove from selection Ctrl + left click Drill into an assembly Alt + Shift + left click Add route point Alt + left click Route context menu Right click

Middle-button look is available when configured. The default look button is the right mouse button.

docs.title: Workbench shortcuts
docs.text: Action Default Find navigation target Ctrl + P Find action Ctrl + Shift + P Navigate back Alt + ← Navigate forward Alt + → Save document Ctrl + S Save as Ctrl + Shift + S Close document Ctrl + W New document Ctrl + N Open file Ctrl + O Compile F5 Undo Ctrl + Z Redo Ctrl + Shift + Z or Ctrl + Y

docs.title: Rebinding
docs.text:
Open Settings → Input and change the action, not the physical key in a tutorial. The saved bindings are read from assets/config/keybindings.json in a source checkout and from the user settings location in a packaged build.

A lesson that uses input_hint("forward") will display the new key. A lesson that hardcodes a key name is not using the controller-owned binding contract.

docs.title: Gamepad and alternate input
docs.text: The input layer maps semantic intents, so an alternate device or a remapped keyboard supplies the same actions. The UI and lessons consume the intent, not the raw key. If an added device does not respond, check that it is mapped to the same intent in the input settings.
